# Microbial keratitis (bacterial, fungal)
Microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening bacterial or fungal infection of the cornea. Usually unilateral, it can cause moderate to severe pain, redness, potentially severe photophobia, discharge and blurred vision. The most likely cause is contact lens wear but others include corneal exposure, ocular injury and surgery.
This Clinical Management Guideline outlines the aetiology, signs and symptoms and evidence-based recommendations for diagnosing and treating microbial keratitis. It outlines the signs that indicate when less severe cases can be managed with antibiotic therapy and those likely to require emergency referral.

...

## What is microbial keratitis?
This is a serious condition in which the cornea (the clear protective layer at the front of the eye) becomes infected. The usual cause is contact lens wear, but infection of the cornea can also happen when there is abnormal exposure of the eye, for example if the eyelids are not blinking normally, loss of sensation in the eye surface, following injury or surgery, insufficient tears (dry eye), and in people whose immune system is not functioning properly.
The infection is usually caused by bacteria, although some cases are caused by fungi.
Microbial keratitis is a very serious condition. It usually begins suddenly with redness and pain in one eye.  The eye waters and there may be a discharge.  Light may hurt the eye, making it difficult to open. The vision of the eye may be blurred.
The optometrist will usually see a cloudy area on the normally clear cornea where the infection is present. There may also be an open sore (ulcer) on the surface of the cornea. Inflammation may also spread to the front part of the eye.

## How is microbial keratitis managed?
Microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening emergency. In the case of small ulcers with a low risk of sight-threatening complications the optometrist may begin treatment with antibiotic eye drops. More serious cases will need to be referred on the same day to an ophthalmologist (specialist eye doctor). Contact lens wearers should be advised not to discard their lenses or lens cases as these may be needed to help identify the cause of the infection.
The ophthalmologist may take a small sample from the ulcer to find out what is causing the infection and will begin treatment with antibiotic eye drops. These will need to be put into the eye very frequently. The patient may need to stay in hospital so that treatment can continue day and night. If the infection is caused by a fungus, the treatment will usually be with anti-fungal eye drops and in some cases with tablets.
When the infection is controlled, steroid eye drops may be prescribed. If the infection was contact lens related, the patient will be given advice on whether it is safe to wear lenses again.
[Visit 'Look after your eyes'](https://lookafteryoureyes.org/)

...

## Last updated
The signs section now highlights the features that should raise suspicion of fungal keratitis. The non-pharmacological management section has been updated to emphasise the importance of contact lens wear and care compliance to reduce the risk of microbial keratitis. The pharmacological section has been updated to consider the use of a topical cycloplegic to relieve pain from ciliary spasm.

# Conjunctivitis - infective: Scenario: Management in primary care
## Scenario: Management in primary care
### How do I manage a person with infective conjunctivitis in primary care?
* **Acute (non-herpetic) viral conjunctivitis**
+ Reassure the person that most cases of acute, infectious conjunctivitis are self-limiting and do not require antimicrobial treatment — viral (non-herpetic) conjunctivitis usually resolves within one to two weeks without treatment.
+ Advise the person that symptoms may be eased with self-care measures such as:

...

- Washing hands frequently with soap and water.
- Using separate towels and flannels.
- Avoiding close contact with others especially if they are a healthcare professional or child care provider – they may be infectious for up to 14 days from onset.
- The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) does not recommend an exclusion period from school, nursery or childminders unless an outbreak or cluster of cases occurs.

...

+ If the person re-attends with symptoms of conjunctivitis, consider sending swabs for viral PCR (for adenovirus and _Herpes simplex_ virus [HSV]) and bacterial culture and if appropriate, offer empirical topical antibiotics. See the section on [Prescribing](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/prescribing-information/) for further information.
+ Consider discussion with/referral to ophthalmology if symptoms persist for more than 7–10 days after initiating treatment.
* **Acute bacterial conjunctivitis**
+ Advise the person that most cases of bacterial conjunctivitis are self-limiting and resolve within 5–7 days without treatment.
+ Treat with topical antibiotics if severe or circumstances require rapid resolution.
A delayed treatment strategy may be appropriate — advise the person to initiate topical antibiotics if symptoms have not resolved within 3 days. Options for topical antibiotics include:
- Chloramphenicol 0.5% drops — apply 1 drop 2 hourly for 2 days, then reduce frequency depending on the severity of infection (3-4 times daily is usually sufficient for less severe infection).
Continue use until 48 hours after infection has cleared.
- Chloramphenicol 1% ointment — apply 3-4 times daily. Continue use until 48 hours after infection has cleared.
- Fusidic acid 1% eye drops — apply 1 drop twice daily. Continue use until 48 hours after infection has cleared.

...

- If the person re-attends with ongoing symptoms of conjunctivitis, consider sending swabs for viral PCR (for adenovirus and _Herpes simplex_ ) and bacterial culture, and consider offering empirical topical antibiotics if these have not already been tried. For further information, see the section on [Prescribing](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/prescribing-information/) .
- Consider referral to ophthalmology if symptoms persist for more than 7 to 10 days after initiating treatment.
* **Conjunctivitis associated with contact lens wear**
+ If topical fluorescein does not identify any corneal staining and the person does not require [referral to ophthalmology](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/management/referral/) :
- Advise them to immediately stop contact lens use.
- Advise regular bathing/cleaning of the eyelids with cotton wool soaked in sterile saline or boiled and cooled water to remove any discharge.
- Advise that contant lense use should be avoided until all symptoms of the infection have gone.
- Treat the infection — consider use of a topical antibiotic effective against Gram –ve organisms, such as an aminoglycoside (e.g. gentamycin) or a quinolone (e.g. levofloxacin or moxifloxacin).
- Arrange follow-up as described above.
+ Have a low threshold for [referral to ophthalmology](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/management/referral/) if there is any suspicion of corneal involvement as this is a potentially sight-threatening condition.

#### Basis for recommendation
The recommendations on the management of infective conjunctivitis in primary care are largely based on expert opinion in the American Academy of Ophthalmology guideline _Conjunctivitis preferred practice pattern_ [ [AAO, 2019](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the _GP Handbook - Common eye condition management_ from the Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust [ [Moorfields Eye Hospital,
2017](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the College of Optometrists guidelines _Conjunctivitis (viral, non-herpetic)_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2020](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ], _Conjunctivitis (bacterial)_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2021b](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ] _Conjunctivitis, Chlamydial (adult inclusion conjunctivitis)_ [
[College of Optometrists 2021](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ] and _Ophthalmia neonatorum_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2021a](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the College of Optometrists _Urgency of referrals table_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2022](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the Royal College of General Practitioners (RCGP) guideline

...

##### Acute (non-herpetic) viral conjunctivitis
* The recommendation on avoidance of antibiotic use in suspected viral (non-herpetic) conjunctivitis is based on expert opinion:
+ Topical antibiotics are not appropriate in viral conjunctivitis and may cause adverse reactions such as allergy or toxicity — repeated use can affect the resistance patterns of normal ocular flora [ [Azari, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [Usher, 2014](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [College of Optometrists,
2020](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
+ Artificial tears, lubricating ointments, and/or topical antihistamines may be useful to alleviate symptoms [ [College of Optometrists, 2020](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
* Follow-up is also necessary to rule out differential diagnoses and to monitor for painful or sight-compromising corneal involvement or development of conjunctival pseudomembrane, both of which necessitate referral to ophthalmology [ [College of Optometrists, 2020](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
* Referral to ophthalmology should be made if symptoms are persistent after 7 to 10 days to reduce the risk of complications [ [Azari, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].

##### Acute bacterial conjunctivitis
* The recommendation that topical antibiotics should not be routinely prescribed unless special circumstances require shorter symptom duration is based on guidelines from the American Academy of Ophthalmology [ [AAO, 2019](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ] and the Royal College of General Practitioners [ [RCGP, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
+ A Cochrane review [ [Sheikh et al, 2012](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ] of 11 randomized controlled trials (n = 3673) found that although acute bacterial conjunctivitis is often self-limiting, use of antibiotic eye drops is associated with quicker resolution of symptoms in comparison to placebo.
+ Patient education is important when prescribing topical antibiotics for a self-limiting condition [ [RCGP, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
* Delayed antibiotic prescribing for 3 days is recommended by the RCGP as this has been associated with reduced antibiotic use:
+ A randomized controlled trial (n = 307) looking at different management strategies for acute infective conjunctivitis (comparing immediate antibiotic treatment, no antibiotics or delayed antibiotics) found that a delayed treatment strategy was better than withholding antibiotics and similar to providing immediate antibiotics in terms of duration of symptoms.
Prescribing strategies did not appear to affect the severity of symptoms [ [Everitt, 2006](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
+ A meta-analysis of data from 3 randomized controlled trials (n = 622) found that topical antibiotics are of limited use in acute infective conjunctivitis and most people got better without them [ [Jefferis, 2011](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
* The recommendations on choice of topical antibiotic in treatment of acute bacterial conjunctivitis are based on guidelines from the American Academy of Ophthalmologists (AAO) [ [AAO, 2019](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ], the College of Optometrists [ [College of Optometrists, 2021b](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ], Public Health England _Managing common infections: guidance

...

+ The AAO and the College of Optometrists state that there is no clinical evidence to suggest superiority of any particular antibiotic to treat bacterial conjunctivitis [ [AAO, 2019](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [College of Optometrists, 2021b](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
+ However, Public Health England states that after conservative measures, chloramphenicol should be used second-line and fusidic acid third-line as it has less activity against Gram negative organisms [ [PHE, 2021](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
